title: No Wash, #1! QB House Fit Stations & Opened 760+ Shops｜Curio Archive
description:
You have probably spotted QB House tucked inside a train or subway station—no hair washing, no phone bookings, and just a green, yellow, and red signal light outside. Think cutting hair washing was only about saving ten minutes and utility bills? The real moat rivals could not match was eliminating water and drain pipes—unlocking old stationmaster offices and dead corners right in commuter traffic!
For anyone who has passed a 10-minute barbershop and wondered how a bare-bones model scaled to 767 stores worldwide and over 300 million visits.

This episode starts with an overslept business meeting at a luxury barbershop in the 1990s. See how an industry outsider tested his bold idea in value-conscious Osaka and scored 30% trial interest—six times his goal—then spent three years refining angled seating with scale models. Using ruthless "¥100 per minute" subtraction, he cut phones, umbrella stands, and cash counters, pioneered hair-salon ticket vending machines (installing two per shop inspired by standing soba counters), and added sensor-driven three-color wait lights. Discover how a hanging gas-station nozzle inspired the overhead "Air Washer" hair vacuum, cutting fit-out costs to one-third without floor plumbing and opening the first shop in Kanda Mitoshiro on November 1, 1996. Finally, follow the 3.3-square-meter "QB Shell" pod to Singapore and Hong Kong, Taiwan's 2012 launch and six-month LogiSCut training school, barcode-to-vacuum staffing analytics (averaging 12 minutes 15 seconds), 300 million cumulative visits in Japan in 2024, the February 2025 ¥1,400 price update (opening the ¥100 monthly discount to all ages at the time), and FY2026/6 consolidated revenue of ¥27.15 billion as QB House marks its 30th anniversary across 767 global stores.

This channel has no affiliation or sponsorship with any company or organization mentioned. All timelines, store counts, and financial figures are sourced from the public primary and media references below.

Illustrations in this episode were generated with AI.

q001.text: QB House cut hair washing to become Japan's top station cut chain!

q002.text: No cashier or phone—just green, yellow, red lights outside.

q003.text: After the cut, an overhead vacuum cleans you up—out in ten minutes!

q004.text: Barbers added washes and massages; QB House stripped them away.

q005.text: Think no wash only saves time? Never digging the floor is the key!

q006.text: This subtraction grew it to over 760 stores in eight countries.

q007.text: Hundreds of millions of Japan visits reshaped haircuts.

q008.text: Yet in 1996, it began as one doubted shop.

q009.text: Today, let's see how cutting the hair wash let QB House pack barbershops into train stations.

q010.text: This haircut shift began with a late 1990s meeting.

q011.text: The founder leased Tokyo dental clinics and gear—a total outsider.

q012.text: Upscale barbers took 4000 yen and a full hour.

q013.text: No wash, towel, or massage: 30 minutes, still 4000 yen!

q014.text: Another time, he napped under the hot towel during full service and arrived late!

q015.text: Frustrated, he asked: why pay for extras you never wanted?

q016.text: That 30-minute cut was mostly chat—real cutting took only ten minutes!

q017.text: Idea: 10 minutes, 1000 yen, no wash, cut only!

q018.text: Crazy from an outsider—would picky customers buy in?

q019.text: Not Tokyo—he surveyed value-savvy Osaka shoppers instead.

q020.text: He polled Namba, office-hub Umeda, and Senri New Town.

q021.text: Hoping for 5 percent, he got 30 percent—six times his goal!

q022.text: Old rules let barber guilds block low prices, stalling him for three years.

q023.text: Waiting, his team used scale models to save every centimeter.

q024.text: In narrow shops, they angled two rows of chairs—shrinking the floor space needed,

q025.text: and stopping customers from locking eyes in the opposite mirror! But how do you profit at that price?

q026.text: Full seats: 100 yen a minute, 6000 an hour!

q028.text: So he cut phones, umbrella stands, magazines, and TVs!

q029.text: Coats and umbrellas go straight into lockers behind each mirror.

q030.text: He even made salon history by bringing in prepay ticket vending machines.

q031.text: Stylists never touch cash or make change—keeping their hands strictly on the scissors.

q032.text: He saw a broken machine freeze a whole standing soba shop.

q033.text: So even tiny shops got two machines—sales could never stop.

q034.text: Remember that three-color light outside? How did it replace phone bookings?

q035.text: Pressure sensors under the waiting bench automatically switch the light based on headcount!

q036.text: Green: no wait, yellow: short, red: 15 minutes plus!

q037.text: Each seat had a 10-minute hourglass for factory pace.

q038.text: One snag remained: without washing, how do you clear loose hair?

q039.text: Towels leave you itchy, and tiny shops can't fit vacuums!

q040.text: The team racked their brains for a year and a half over where to hide the unit and cords.

q041.text: Then he passed a Japanese gas station with overhead hoses, looked up at the nozzles, and cracked it!

q042.text: He hid the motor inside the ceiling and dropped a flexible hose straight down overhead.

q043.text: That created the signature hair vacuum hose, freeing up massive floor space!

q044.text: Sharing one hose per two chairs failed, so each got one.

q045.text: No sinks or fancy chairs cut build-out costs to a third!

q046.text: Speed and cost were just the start—no floor plumbing was the killer move!

q047.text: Normal salons bury water and drain pipes—strictly banned in stations.

q048.text: Even better, he eyed old stationmaster offices and storage!

q049.text: These dry, empty rooms sat right in the path of daily commuters!

q050.text: Railways earned rent; QB House got traffic!

q051.text: Then rules eased right in late 1995!

q052.text: He immediately pitched train stations—only to get turned down flat!

q053.text: Rejected for having no track record, how did he win the railway operators over?

q054.text: In 1996, a Tokyo Kanda street shop proved sales!

q055.text: Opening day poured yet packed out—drawing five TV crews.

q056.text: Railways bought in—by late 1997 he had twelve shops!

q057.text: Next came malls, breaking the men-only image to reach twenty percent women!

q058.text: Across hundreds of shops, under one percent closed for weak sales!

q059.text: Profits bred envy, and copycat cut shops flooded streets!

q060.text: Suppliers cloned the vacuums, selling rivals the full setup.

q061.text: Stations full and clones everywhere—where could QB House grow next?

q062.text: It made a 3.3-square-meter pod—assembled in half a day—for office corners!

q063.text: Could this tiny pod really take off in Japan?

q064.text: Surprisingly, no waiting area broke Japan's barber rules!

q065.text: Blocked at home, QB House took pods to foreign malls!

q066.text: Singapore in 2002, then Hong Kong 3 years later!

q067.text: Even at triple rent it won Japan's Good Design Award!

q068.text: Taiwan in 2012, now 42 shops—plus the US!

q070.text: Going global wasn't enough: where do you find top stylists?

q071.text: Old salons keep rookies washing for years, starving copycats.

q072.text: In 2012, it built a school turning craft into logic!

q073.text: Even total beginners pass and hit the floor after six months.

q074.text: Cutting only gives stylists four times the practice!

q075.text: Schools expanded to Hong Kong, Taipei, and Taichung.

q076.text: Better yet, skipping washes solved salon stylist burnout!

q077.text: Dry hands prevent eczema, and no sink bending helps stylists stay!

q078.text: 720 liters saved per guest—over 1.3 billion a year!

q079.text: Bills plunged too, earning a strong eco image.

q080.text: Space, water, talent solved—QB House had one final weapon.

q081.text: Buy a ticket, and every step feeds precision data!

q082.text: A timer starts at barcode scan and stops when the vacuum shuts off.

q083.text: That tracking keeps average cuts at twelve minutes, fifteen seconds!

q084.text: Headquarters spots lunch station peaks and afternoon mall rushes.

q085.text: It even shifts stylists hourly across shops, slashing idle time!

q086.text: In 2017, this won Japan's prestigious Porter Prize.

q087.text: Next year it hit the Tokyo Stock Exchange and boomed!

q089.text: Reused combs cut 659 tons CO2 by 2024!

q090.text: Scale peaked, yet inflation made 1000 yen impossible to hold.

q091.text: With costs and wages rising, how do you raise prices safely?

q094.text: Then, it opened the seniors' 100-yen monthly discount to all ages!

q095.text: Monthly regulars barely felt a price hike at all!

q096.text: Meanwhile, it opened premium shops in Otemachi and Ginza.

q097.text: App waitlists and styling unlocked higher margins.

q098.text: It even launched nine-to-five shops to retain parent stylists!

q099.text: What results did this bring right before its 30th birthday?

q101.text: In Nikkei's survey, it ranked second among all salon chains!

q102.text: On November 1 that year, it marked its thirtieth anniversary.

q103.text: One barber-chair nap ended up rewriting haircuts across Asia.

q104.text: At Tokyo Station or Taipei MRT, cuts are easy as coffee.

q105.text: Yet most people misunderstand subtraction's power.

q106.text: Many think subtraction just means cheap cuts and thin margins.

q107.text: Great subtraction drops old habits and rewrites rules!

q108.text: Drop assumed hardware limits, and your territory explodes.

q109.text: While rivals wage price wars, you're on an open track.

q110.text: A clever idea alone gets copied by richer competitors.

q111.text: Its thirty-year lead wasn't hardware—it was discipline.

q112.text: When speed and quality scale reliably, low prices still win big!

q113.text: That lesson still hits: what bundled extras do you pay for?

q114.text: Brands equate luxury with value, forgetting saving time is worth more.

q115.text: Cut every extra step and perfect the core—that's the hardest to replace.

q116.text: Next time you pass a station corner and spot that glowing green light on a glass door,

q117.text: remember it's a masterclass in subtraction that rewrote the rules of physical space!

q118.text: Ever tried a station QB House? What stood out to you most?
